speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chairman, I move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head Q of the Estimates be reduced by $100." Digitalisation is our present reality and an inevitable future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This transformation is not just about technological upgrades, but fundamentally reshaping our society, economy and way of life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It presents vast economic opportunities, promising a better quality of life for future generations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore has always been unafraid of transformations, having pivoted through multiple strategic ones since our Independence.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is especially meaningful given that this is the year of SG60.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, as we pick up the pace in our march towards a digital future, we must also ensure that our digitally-driven growth must be sustainable, inclusive and safe for all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are several factors that I believe are imperative to a digitally-successful future, namely: world class digital infrastructure, vibrant talent community and ecosystem, widespread adoption by businesses, sustainable and green development, safe and inclusive digital society, and stronger global cooperation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this opening cut, I will focus on world class digital infrastructure, sustainable and green development as well as safe and inclusive digital society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore has always invested heavily in building up our infrastructure ahead of time so that when the wave arrives, we are ready to ride it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Underpinning our digital growth must, therefore, be enabled by high-performing, resilient and secure digital infrastructure, which includes broadband networks, cloud services, data centres and high-performance computing power.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore ranks first in Asia for digital infrastructure in the recent IMD World Digital Competitiveness Ranking.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is no easy feat and only possible because of years of careful planning and hard work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: More importantly, in the digital world, everything runs 24/7.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I note that the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) released the Advisory Guidelines for cloud service providers and data centres last month to enhance their resilience and security.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the key measures in these guidelines and how they help operators uplift their resilience and security measures?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more integrated horizontally and vertically across industries and sectors, as the overall adoption of digital technologies increases, the demand for data centres and higher computing power will increase.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Consequently, the demand for energy will also rise exponentially.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Training advanced AI models, for instance, can emit a carbon footprint comparable to driving a gasoline-powered vehicle for five to 20 miles per unit of processed text.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can we consider having structured programmes to drive the use of energy-efficient algorithms across industries?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can we consider setting more instructive guidelines to advise industries on the preferred type of hardware to be used and standards to adopt when designing software?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is currently one developed by IMDA and Microsoft on software development.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Is there scope for such guidelines to be further expanded?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Despite the geopolitical sensitivities, what can we learn from DeepSeek's experience as it is considered to be cheaper and greener than other AI models?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How will the Government secure more green energy to support a sustainable digital development for Singapore?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Lastly, trust is fundamental in a society and underpinning trust in a digital society is to ensure that it is inclusive and safe for all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For a digital future to truly succeed, Singaporeans must be able to enjoy easy access to digital services and participate meaningfully in the digital economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They should also feel safe when they interact and transact online.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To this end, our Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Digital Development and Information moved a Motion in January last year to "reaffirm our commitment to adopt a whole-of-nation approach to sustain trust by building an inclusive and safe digital society".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Members discussed the imperatives of ensuring an inclusive and safe digital society and put forth 13 calls to action to achieve this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And in ensuring safety, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong mentioned that there will be a new law to protect victims from online harms, when he launched Smart Nation 2.0.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And so, there is new imperative and new urgency for us to do more to protect those who are victimised online.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And, therefore, can the Minister provide more details on how the new law will help address online harms?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As I still have time, please allow me to speak in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Chairman, going towards a digital economy is a must in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, we must continue to make our digital economy green and sustainable; and second, ensure deeper participation from our citizens so they can share the fruits of progress.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Based on the second point, we need to ensure that we can build a safe and inclusive digital society where citizens can participate meaningfully in the development of the digital economy with peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope the Minister can update us on these calls.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope the Minister can provide us with more information on this. : Sir, our pursuit for digital growth and realising a digital future will mean nothing if it cannot be sustained and if our people do not feel safe or get to enjoy the benefits of digitalisation.

speaker: The Chairman
text: You can take all of the rest of your cuts together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I talked about both the opportunities and challenges that come along with that.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I also shared that there are several factors that I believe are imperative to a digitally successful future, namely: world-class digital infrastructure, vibrant talent community and ecosystem, widespread adoption by businesses, sustainable and green development, safe and inclusive digital society, and stronger global cooperation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Here, I will talk about talents and ecosystem, support for businesses and global cooperation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Within NAIS 2.0, people and communities form an important system.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: No digital future can be realised without the right human capital.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We must nurture our young, build our native talent pipeline and attract the brightest minds from across the globe.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Not only do we want to build up our Singaporeans to have what it takes to capitalise on the opportunities in and out of Singapore, we want them to learn and spar with top talents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: And by fostering a vibrant community of talents, research institutes and enterprises, ideas can cross-fertilise, collaborations can happen and we can create a virtuous cycle of innovation that benefits both our economy and our people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Public and private partnerships, along with robust peer-to-peer collaboration, are essential to provide the meaningful opportunities that will keep talent anchored in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Hence, can the Minister provide an update about what is being done to strengthen our talent pool and enhance the "staying power" of these talents and community of partners in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Next, our local enterprises are a key part of the engine driving our economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We must help our local enterprises to adopt new and impactful technologies, so that the power of these innovations can be fully unleashed to benefit our economy and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Over the years, the Government has taken significant steps to support these enterprises in adopting new technologies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: However, with the breakthrough of Gen AI models, such as those that have emerged recently, we must redouble our efforts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It is imperative that enterprises across sectors integrate AI into their core strategies and operations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: And a more targeted approach for specific sectors and for businesses with different digital maturity is needed to help them move along.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How does IMDA plan to support businesses at different stages of digital maturity in adopting and leveraging Gen AI technologies, and what specific benefits would the Minister anticipate for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) from these new initiatives?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: At the same time, geopolitical tensions, particularly the United States (US)-China rivalry, pose challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Companies will need clarity and assurances when choosing which Gen AI platforms to adopt.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: For example, some may have concerns about the use of DeepSeek's AI models due to potential implications from US sanctions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As we navigate these complex dynamics, there may be scope for us to provide clearer guidelines and support for our enterprises to adopt technology without fear of reprise or sanctions from either of the major powers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Building on hon Member Henry Kwek's point made during the Budget debate, I agree that it is important to ensure that we are able to build up a model that can take into consideration our local social values, ethical standards and other more local factors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: If we take a look at DeepSeek, we also know that DeepSeek itself, hailed as a breakthrough, was also distilled from many other AI models as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Therefore, I would like to ask whether it is possible for Singapore to also develop or distill our own AI model, so that our companies can leverage on this and to continue to grow and develop with greater sense of assurance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We were also told that the Ministry had established key performance indicators (KPIs) for SPH Media Trust.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For FY2024/2025, what objective criteria did the Ministry set for these KPIs that were not reached?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More specifically, were these KPIs lowered or were they increased?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Has SPH Media Trust fared any better since last year?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share data on print and digital subscriptions to its English and vernacular titles, respectively, over the last two years?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I had also asked the Minister about the way the Ministry presented its subsidies to SPH Media Trust in the Budget book, and whether there was a simpler way for the public to track and understand the KPIs the Ministry had set for SPH Media Trust.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This point is important given the size of the subsidy granted to the mainstream media.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After all, as the Minister would agree, the proof of the pudding is in the eating.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the Ministry conduct local surveys to gauge the public response to our local media outlets?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And if so, how does it make the decision to deploy taxpayer dollars to those media outlets that rank less satisfactorily in the public eye?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What other objective KPIs does the Ministry keep track of to ensure that the taxpayer dollars for SPH Media is purposefully spent?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Chairman: Ms Hany Soh, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While advancements in technology and AI bring about new opportunities, they also present new challenges and competition.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Take the news, media and entertainment spheres, for example.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Consumers worldwide have been increasingly moving towards online streaming services and non-traditional sources, such as social media.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This came after a reduction of its headcount by 10%, or nearly 2,000 roles.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Its long-time flagship current affairs interview programme, HARDtalk, was also axed as a result.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: CNN also announced its plan to lay off 6% of its workforce in January earlier this year, as it revamps its schedule and digital strategy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This followed having already cut 100 jobs, or about 3% of its workforce, last summer as it reorganised its news gathering operations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During my interactions with union members who are in the broadcasting industry in my capacity as the advisor of the Singapore Union of Broadcasting Employees, I picked up on one of their concerns that job restructuring is inevitable as Singaporeans, like the rest of the world, are consuming media from across a range of digital sources and platforms, and there is thus a rapid decline in consumption of its content from traditional analogue media platforms.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Against this evolving backdrop, how does MDDI intend to support our Public Service Media entities, ensuring that they remain relevant and maintain or improve audience outreach, given ongoing technological disruptions and the proliferation of information sources?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   Over the years, the Government has been helping vulnerable groups integrate into the digital society through various initiatives, such as DigitalAccess@Home, Seniors Go Digital and Mobile Access for Seniors.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These programmes provide subsidised broadband equipment, raise public awareness about digital technology and offer training to support these groups.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In light of this, could MDDI share the current outcomes of these initiatives?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What progress has Seniors Go Digital made in training seniors to use digital tools?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Additionally, what challenges have been encountered during the implementation of these programmes and what measures have been taken to address them?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Are there plans to further expand this support in the future?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Expand community workshops to provide more personalised digital training for seniors, such as one-on-one tutoring, to meet their learning needs while continuing to enhance their awareness and ability to prevent online scams.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Strengthen support for assistive technologies and training for people with disabilities, possibly by collaborating with business enterprise and professional organisations to provide customised solutions.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Digital inclusion is essential for social equity and progress.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I look forward to the Ministry's response and believe that these efforts will continue to benefit more Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, digitisation is transforming the way we live, work and interact.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: From e-payments to telemedicine and digital Government services, technology has become a cornerstone of our daily life.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore advances, we must ensure that every Singaporean, regardless of age, ability or background, can confidently navigate the online space without fear of exclusion or exploitation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Our digital future must be built on inclusivity, empowerment and safety.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: While many have adapted, others remain digitally vulnerable and lack digital confidence.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: These include seniors struggling with e-services and persons with physical and mental disabilities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: These efforts are commendable and instrumental in closing the digital divide.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: But more needs to be done to reach underserved communities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: A report by the Ministry of Social and Family Development has highlighted the need for design and technological solutions to promote independent living among persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: How can we scale efforts to further bridge the digital divide?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: What strategies are in place to empower citizens with the skills and confidence to use technology safely and effectively?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: How are we ensuring accessibility across all digital platforms, particularly for persons with disabilities?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: How are we strengthening public awareness of online threats, ensuring that Singaporeans can identify and protect themselves against digital risks?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: An inclusive, safe and digitally empowered society is not just a goal.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We must ensure that every Singaporean can access, use and benefit from technology securely and confidently.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gerald Giam, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, some Singaporeans struggle to keep up, whether due to physical limitations, lack of digital literacy or difficulties adapting.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These individuals risk being left behind as more Government and business services move online.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Providing parallel paper applications is not always a solution to digital marginalisation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These officers should guide users through digital applications, helping them to use the systems independently over time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: ServiceSG centres play an important role in guiding citizens through Government e-services, but their officers cannot be expected to know every agency's processes in detail.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While they assist with common digital functions, they are not equipped to handle complex applications like for a Long-Term Visit Pass or public defender.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Government agencies must take responsibility for guiding users through their own systems.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How many seniors have been trained and to what extent has their digital literacy improved?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are there plans to expand the programme to reach more citizens?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Beyond basic training, digital inclusion efforts should also ensure that seniors and other digitally marginalised groups can more confidently use essential platforms, including communication apps that connect them with the family, businesses and Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I was asked about my satisfaction with life, the economy and my neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I was also asked to rate whether I believe the Government makes decisions in the best interest of Singapore, whether it takes my opinion seriously and if there are enough channels to voice my views.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I was also asked to rate the quality of the Armed Forces, Civil Service, mainstream media and online media, as well as my confidence in the Police and the Courts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There were questions on affordability, whether I find housing, healthcare, public transport and education affordable.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I was asked about competition from foreigners at work, the pace of immigration and the quality of migrants.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, I was asked how strongly I identify as a Singaporean and whether I would migrate to another country for a better quality of life.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When I asked who commissioned the survey, the pollster could not tell me.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More recently, I saw another pollster conducting a similar survey in my neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I also received similar surveys via phone in the past.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are these surveys being commissioned by the Government?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are they used only to shape public policy or are they also used to gauge public sentiment for electoral purposes?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Otherwise, there is a risk that such surveys will be seen as serving partisan interests rather than benefiting Singapore and Singaporeans as a whole.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I emphasised the need for awareness, appropriate interventions and collective efforts from the Government, families and society to create a safer and more constructive online environment.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last year, I highlighted the pervasiveness of digital technology in exposing youths to harmful online content and how unrealistic body standards being purveyed through mainstream and social media platforms have become a source of mental health strain for our society.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The online world has become an indispensable part of our lives, offering opportunities for networking, knowledge sharing and content creation.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, it must also be made safer, especially for the young and impressionable.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some have suggested access bans as a solution to online harms, but banning access alone is clearly not the way forward.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, social media bans might generate unintended dangers.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The premise is: young people are adept at using the Internet.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Bans might push them to access social media without their parents' knowledge or prompt them to look for unregulated and hidden areas of the Internet.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I, therefore, reiterate my call to the MDDI to dive deeper into how we can shape an online environment that balances safety as well as opportunities for growth.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After all, our digital space should remain a constructive platform for young people to network, share knowledge and create content, one that is safer and more conducive for everyone.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chairman, online safety is a work in progress and perhaps, will always remain so.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The inaugural Online Safety Assessment Report bears this out.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think MDDI has done a lot to advance online safety for Singaporean users and our online safety laws are landmark.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I have a few questions for the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, how would the Ministry work with the designated social media services to ensure that they do much better in acting on user reports and take down harmful content much more quickly?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Two, would the Ministry consider stepping up punitive measures on the social media services?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, I love the libraries when I was growing up.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A visit to the National Library at Fort Canning or the regional libraries was always a real treat.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, therefore, rise to invite the Ministry to update the House on how our public libraries will be evolving to support a future-ready Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In particular, libraries have long been a cornerstone of community enrichment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, the digital age calls for more innovative approaches to learning.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What new initiatives can we expect to see in our libraries that will encourage greater tech adoption and skills acquisition for all Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Furthermore, how will these initiatives be scaled up for different age groups, especially our seniors, so that everyone, regardless of digital fluency, can benefit?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Libraries should not just be repositories of books, but living, breathing testbeds of new knowledge and digital hands-on experiences.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I look forward to hearing how the Ministry plans to bring these transformative opportunities to the heart of our communities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In our interconnected world, social media and digital platforms are powerful tools for community building.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, they can also be fertile breeding grounds for harmful discourse, misinformation and polarising narratives that threaten our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have long prided ourselves on our cohesive society and we must not let online vitriol undermine our unity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Youths, in particular, are vulnerable to the negative influences in these digital spaces.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could the Minister please share the Ministry’s strategic efforts to foster civic-mindedness on the Internet, be it through digital literacy programmes, collaborative initiatives with community groups or targeted policies encouraging responsible online behaviour?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, how will the Ministry ensure our digital services truly leave no one behind, especially our seniors and people with disabilities?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we forge ahead with smart initiatives and digital transformation, how will these advances remain equitable and accessible to vulnerable groups in our society?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We know that technology can be intimidating at times, even exclusionary, if not implemented thoughtfully.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will the Ministry, therefore, be introducing new standards or guidelines to ensure our websites, apps and other digital resources are user-friendly for individuals with varying needs?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have worked with many of them on various projects, and I can attest to their passion and dedication in making lives more closely connected and digitally-efficient, yet also so tremendously people-centred.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: During the January Ministerial Statement, Minister Josephine Teo clarified that scammers are not known to directly use NRIC numbers to steal or unlock valuables.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Still, NRIC numbers continue to serve as a gateway to accessing personal, but not secret, information in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Take, for example, the Eligibility Checker for the Matched Retirement Savings Scheme, on the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board website.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It may not be obvious how this information could be misused.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: But in the hands of scammers, it could be used to build credibility and manipulate vulnerable individuals through social engineering tactics.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate the CPF Board's intent to make the eligibility checks convenient.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: However, with scams becoming more sophisticated, should we not re-consider the right balance between security and convenience more carefully?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We must act with foresight to stay ahead of emerging threats.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: With its deep expertise in data protection, MDDI is best placed to help our Government agencies develop the instinct for proactive data security.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the increasing adoption of digital technologies and services and Singapore's Smart Nation ambition, ensuring digital resilience is essential in building and maintaining trust, amongst citizens as well as businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Our cybersecurity ecosystem, the Next Generation Nationwide Broadband Network (NextGen NBN) and infrastructure development, our education and workforce development, digital governance and innovation play pivotal roles in Singapore's digital resilience strategy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As digital technologies become more pervasive, the risks of cyberattacks and sophistication of cyber threats are increasing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The demand for skills in cybersecurity, AI and emerging technologies continue to grow, both public sector and businesses are facing talent shortage.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To ensure robust digital infrastructure, Singapore will need to invest in infrastructure upgrades and readiness.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The rapid pace of technological advancements will require the regulatory and policy frameworks to be agile and adaptable, to ensure that regulations are supportive of innovation while still providing the necessary safeguards.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, how is Singapore preparing to stay ahead of emerging digital threats and having an adaptive digital strategy?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And can MDDI share what the strategic priorities for enhancing our digital resilience in Singapore is?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, the adoption of AI and innovation offer substantial growth opportunities for businesses across sectors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: By adopting AI solutions, businesses can unlock new revenue streams, enhance customer experiences, optimise operations and mitigate risks.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As shared in the Ministry of Trade and Industry's (MTI's) COS yesterday, AI adoption is increasing across different industries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The landscape for businesses in the drive to adopt AI solutions is both promising and challenging.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, how is the Government creating an enabling environment to support businesses to actively, and I emphasise the word "actively", embrace and implement AI solutions to enhance competitiveness and to drive growth?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How are Singapore businesses progressing in the digital adoption and embracing of AI solutions for their businesses?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A significant challenge for businesses in their adoption of AI solutions is the shortage and competition for skilled AI professionals.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These include computing power, data storage and cloud services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Having access to high quality data is also essential for successful AI adoption as data is an essential building block for training AI models.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As AI adoption grows, businesses must ensure that they use AI responsibly and ethically, including how they handle data privacy, bias and transparency.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is crucial in building and maintaining trust.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore's vision for a Smart Nation and our commitment to digital transformation for sustainable growth require us to have a strong talent pool of digital expertise and capabilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A key pillar of Singapore's digital strategy is accelerating AI development and deployment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A critical factor in advancing AI capabilities is the development of a strong talent pool.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The landscape of AI expertise and capabilities is dynamic and rapidly evolving, with countries around the world making significant investments in AI research, development and talent acquisition.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, how is the Government ensuring a strong pipeline and retention of technical expertise and AI capabilities, within the public sector and the wider Singapore ecosystem?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Considering Singapore's limited resources, how are we building these capabilities and what are the key consideration in helping us leapfrog in AI innovations?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In a global competitive landscape for AI talent, how is Singapore progressing in the development and attraction of top AI expertise and capabilities?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, AI is rapidly transforming industries, reshaping jobs and redefining essential skills.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This shift is not limited to large enterprises.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: AI proficiency should be a universal workforce asset, not a specialised skill limited to a few.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Education institutions are stepping up, with initiatives like Ngee Ann Polytechnic's Gen AI courses, equipping professionals with practical AI skills.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Yet, SME adoption of such training remains uncertain.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, in healthcare to predict and manage disease outbreaks and growing medical conditions, in infrastructure to do smart traffic planning, in social services to speed up document processing or detect fraudulent activities, in customer service and citizen engagement.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government as a lead user can also provide a base load for emerging AI infrastructure, and develop and stress test emerging responsible AI frameworks are tailored to our values.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, the Government is already using AI in use cases, like traffic management.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is the value that has been created?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What steps is the Government taking to accelerate the adoption of AI and Gen AI, and value creation through AI in Government?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For true enterprise value creation, enterprises must go beyond to use AI to reshape their critical core business processes, such as AI-driven fault detection, or to invent new products and services, such as by charging their customers AI credits on a pay-as-you-go basis for new AI features.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Only then can we drive true value creation through higher revenue growths, dramatically transform operational efficiencies and enhance customer experience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: On this front, enterprise adoption of AI in Singapore remains very uneven, especially amongst SMEs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Having done some research on this topic, I can share that the main challenges are setting the right ambition and alignment on AI, scaling from AI proof-of-concept to generating value at-scale, and finding the right talent.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Smaller companies also find access to Cloud and AI infrastructure expensive.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Sharael Taha, you can take your five cuts together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While Singapore is building deep capabilities in AI, cybersecurity and other emerging technologies, these skills are not just critical for tech professionals, but also basic end user knowledge is increasingly essential for the general workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we strive to develop a workforce with deep expertise, it is equally important to uplift the broader workforce with foundational digital and AI skills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: AI should not remain a niche skillset for a select few.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Rather, it should become as commonplace as the use of Microsoft Word or Excel in today's workplace.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond the tech sector, AI has the potential to enhance productivity and enable faster and better decision-making, particularly for SMEs too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we accelerate the development of AI literacy and digital skills across the broader workforce, ensuring that workers, whether in retail, logistics, professional services or any other industry, can harness AI to drive productivity, scale their businesses and stay competitive in the global market?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many SMEs lack the budget to build in-house digital teams to hire AI talent to identify and implement AI opportunities in their businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How is the Government supporting SMEs in leveraging AI to boost productivity, enhance decision-making and scale effectively through the adoption of AI enabled solutions?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore aspires to be a global leader in AI adoption, innovation and digital technology solutions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on these collaborations?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we further encourage companies to develop or establish their AI capabilities in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond schemes and grants, building the right ecosystem is crucial to attracting and sustaining AI-driven developments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This requires not only skilled talent and cutting-edge infrastructure, such as an ultra-fast broadband network, but also effective matching of technology to business needs, alongside the necessary safeguards to prevent misuse.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the same time, the very infrastructure and expertise that enables AI innovation can also be exploited for criminal activities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What safeguards are in place to prevent misuse by malicious actors and ensure the integrity of our AI ecosystem?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many SMEs lack the budget to build in-house cybersecurity teams or hire talent with deep expertise in cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we assist SMEs to upgrade their cybersecurity posture?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The support for our vernacular media has enabled the platforms to transform and provide many innovative digital products to engage the community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Berita Harian, in particular, has been able to provide many media offerings for the Malay language speaker, not only in Singapore, but in the region.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is important as it provides the Singapore Malays' perspective on current affairs issues in the region.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How has this increased the viewership of Berita Harian and how can we further assist our vernacular papers to reach out to the much larger Malay speakers in the region?

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their cuts.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, the Prime Minister launched Smart Nation 2.0 – a refresh of our vision for Singapore to use technology to uplift the lives of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, I will elaborate on our efforts in four areas: (a) how we support our workforce to succeed in the age of AI; (b) how we keep Singaporeans safe by fighting harmful online activities; (c) how we protect our cyberspace against malicious attacks; and (d) how we preserve trust in our information space (infospace) by strengthening public service media.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, may I ask the Clerks to distribute the package of handouts?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL app.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Jessica Tan, Miss Rachel Ong and Mr Sharael Taha also raised concerns about its impact on workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are real and will be with us for some time, because we are only at the very early stages of AI adoption globally.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: People all over the world would like to know who will be impacted and how.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While there is no perfect clarity, there are ways in which we can help.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The first is to recognise that many jobs will still be around.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The risk is not that these jobs will be lost to AI, but that they are lost to another country or city that is more competitive than us.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our most important task, therefore, is to help as many people and businesses as we can become more productive, with the use of AI.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We want to become a nation of competent and confident AI users.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In doing so, we can maintain Singapore's economic competitiveness and retain more good jobs here.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members will see that Singapore is well-regarded and well-placed to benefit from widespread AI adoption.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have established strong partnerships with tech companies, like Amazon Web Services, Databricks, Google and Oracle.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under this expansion, workers in all sectors, be it manufacturing or retail, can learn how to use tools, such as ChatGPT and CoPilot.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will help them to enhance their productivity at work, even if they have no background in technology.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second thing we must recognise is that AI will create new jobs even as it replaces some existing ones.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Members have highlighted, our next most important task is to deepen our AI capabilities and anchor more new jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This means growing our pool of AI practitioners, which includes data scientists, machine learning engineers and more.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Take, for example, the need for AI safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As AI adoption grows, there will be greater demand for AI testing and assurance service providers, just as the widespread information technology (IT) adoption led to greater demand for IT auditors.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Estimates of the market for such testing, inspection and certification services vary, but they would be in the billions in time to come.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Singapore believes in the importance of good AI governance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We were one of the first in the world to introduce a testing framework and software toolkit, AI Verify.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Just last month, I launched the Global AI Assurance Pilot of the AI Verify Foundation to promote best practices in the testing of models using Gen AI.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These efforts can help to grow the AI testing industry here and create new jobs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The AI Centres of Excellence that MDDI and MTI worked closely together to set up will catalyse more demand for AI practitioners, by the hundreds if not thousands.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To meet demand, we need to grow a strong pipeline of AI practitioners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To this end, we will expand our efforts under IMDA's TechSkills Accelerator (TeSA).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also explore ways to expand the AI Apprenticeship Programme together with AI Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Seow Yuxin studied business and started her career in Regional Operations for an e-commerce platform.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: She did not work on AI systems directly, but the role sparked her interest in the field.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After seeing her husband and brother-in-law go through the AI Apprenticeship Programme, she took a leap of faith and enrolled in the programme.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I spoke to Yuxin recently and was pleased to learn that she has pivoted to a new role in a new company delivering AI and data-driven solutions to other organisations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are determined to keep AI opportunities open and inclusive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Yuxin shows that one can access AI opportunities even without a STEM background.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will aim to support more Singaporeans like her to fulfil their AI aspirations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As a Government, we will always put our people at the heart of all we do and that includes our AI plans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope these efforts reassure Members of our support for Singaporeans to make the most of AI.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides succeeding with AI, we want Singaporeans to feel safe when they go online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But this is not something the Government alone can achieve.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Social media platforms must do their part, no different from how all service providers bear some responsibilities towards their users.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why we passed the Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act in 2022 to set out their basic obligations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Like Mr Eric Chua, we believe in adopting a holistic and balanced approach to online safety, particularly for young users.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Where it is useful to do so, we will strengthen regulatory levers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, in January, we issued a new Code of Practice for Online Safety for App Distribution Services.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For the first time, we are introducing measures to ensure that young users under 18 do not access age-inappropriate apps.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Last month, we also published our first ever Online Safety Assessment Report.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To questions raised by Mr Xie Yao Quan, the report showed that the designated social media services made good efforts to put in place baseline user safety measures.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, as he has also pointed out, there are areas for improvement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They should respond more quickly to user reports.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also want to do more to support the victims of online harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: IMDA's report found that, more often than not, platforms fail to take action to remove genuinely harmful content reported to them by victims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One such victim was Jane, and that is not her real name.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At 18, she was horrified to find an image of her face superimposed onto another person's nude body, circulating on an image sharing platform.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Strangers reposted the image and left comments, some of which sexualised or insulted her.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When she reported this to the platform, they took down only the original post but not the reposts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During this ordeal, she felt scared and embarrassed, even blaming herself for posting photos online in the first place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A full decade later, at 29 years old today, Jane continues to question who created that photo of her and if it is still found online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Victims like Jane need more support to find closure.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Victims will be able to request OSC to issue a direction to the platform to take down the offensive content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The platform must also remove existing identical copies on the platform – something they refused to do for Jane.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The new law will also help victims hold their perpetrators accountable.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If they want to sue the perpetrators, they can request OSC to direct the platform to provide information about the perpetrators.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In drafting the new law, the Minister of Law and MDDI have engaged a wide range of stakeholders from industry, academia, community groups and international partners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also invited the public to provide their feedback.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The public consultation findings have been published on the website of Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are heartened by the strong support and useful feedback which will help refine our proposals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Given the complexity and vastness of the digital space, rules and regulations alone are insufficient.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister of State Rahayu will share what citizens can do to protect themselves online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is reflected in the digital domain, where cyber threats have become more severe.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Criminal groups are increasingly going online to look for illicit gains.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Advanced Persistent Threat actors, linked to certain states, are actively seeking to advance their national agenda.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have seen both kinds of activities in our cyberspace.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Last year, a global botnet, which included infected servers and devices around the world, was discovered.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: More details can be found in the handout.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Until the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) participated in an international operation to disrupt this botnet, about 2,700 devices in Singapore had been infected, unbeknownst to their owners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The malicious actors exploited poor cyber hygiene practices to infect devices, including baby monitors and Internet routers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members may ask, so what if the botnet had remained?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Well, it would have meant the devices were vulnerable and personal data belonging to device owners could have been stolen.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: More worryingly, the devices could be used as a standby army, much like our full-time National Servicemen, ready to be deployed into active duty.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Except in this case, it would be foreign state-linked actors using the bots for malicious purposes, which can include targets directed within Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Ms Tin Pei Ling highlighted, international partnerships are critical in combatting such complex threats.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: CSA could act only because it has recognised capabilities and was trusted by its partners to be involved in this international operation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Botnets are just one of the many cyber threats we need to defend against.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why we emphasise the need to safeguard our cybersecurity at multiple levels.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For individuals, we will continue working with industry partners to offer better protection.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One example is the Enhanced Fraud Protection feature under Google Play Protect.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A common scam tactic is to entice victims to download apps from unofficial sources that can inject malware into our devices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With this feature, such download attempts on Android devices will be blocked.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For organisations, the Government is improving the SG Cyber Safe Programme.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How will share more details later.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also agree with Mr Sharael Taha on the need to raise our national cybersecurity posture.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Last year, CSA amended the Cybersecurity Act to require that CII owners report on a larger set of cyber incidents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also expanded CSA's oversight beyond CIIs to other important systems and entities, such as cloud services and data centres.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: More information can be found in the handout.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will share more later.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What I worry about are the organisations that are not covered by such legislation, that are not paying enough attention to cybersecurity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Thankfully, over 500 organisations believe in the importance of cybersecurity and have acted on it by getting their Cyber Essentials and Cyber Trust Marks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But we should raise baseline cybersecurity standards nationally and protect more organisations, especially those of higher risk.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: CSA is, therefore, assessing if more measures are needed, particularly for vendors that may be given access to sensitive data or systems within the Government.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such vendors include cybersecurity penetration testing firms and cybersecurity auditors.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Government may also take the lead to incorporate cybersecurity considerations in our procurement decisions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As the impact of these measures may be non-trivial, CSA plans to engage the industry before deciding.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are also developing a new Code of Practice to require social media companies to prevent and counter abuse of fake content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Against the tide of false information online, we must have trusted sources to turn to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Thankfully, our Public Service Media (PSM) entities remain many Singaporeans' first port of call for credible news.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Straits Times and CNA are amongst our most frequented online news platforms, with more than 40% of Singaporeans reading them weekly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: More importantly, public trust in our mainstream media remains high, with CNA and The Straits Times being the most trusted by Singaporeans at 74% and 73% respectively.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Meanwhile, public trust in mainstream news has fallen in other countries, hovering at 60% or below.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many Singaporeans, including Ms Hany Soh and Mr Sharael Taha, appreciate the efforts of Mediacorp and SPH Media to adapt to changing audience preferences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Against a climate of stiff competition, news fatigue and opaque algorithms on social media platforms, both companies are committed to increase audience reach.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, falling revenues have forced their newsrooms to rationalise.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: SPH Media ceased publication of its Chinese entertainment magazine, U-Weekly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Last October, Mediacorp merged TODAY Online with CNA's Digital newsroom.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Pritam Singh expressed concerns about SPH Media's performance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Like news outlets worldwide, SPH Media's print subscriptions have declined as readers shift to consuming news online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, less than 20% of consumers in advanced countries, including Singapore, now pay for digital news subscriptions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Essentially, they can get it for free and they will continue to enjoy such services for free.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It was only 20% higher two years ago.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: SPH Media will have to continue its pivot to digital news and the Government must support this effort so that our PSM entities can meet audiences where they are.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Despite not meeting all their KPIs last year, SPH Media did not ask to lower their targets.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are determined to maintain their reach and relevance with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In 2024, they maintained their strong overall reach at 70% of Singapore's resident population although youths and vernacular reach dipped.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In line with the funding agreement, MDDI will pro-rate and award the Performance-Linked Incentives accordingly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would suggest respectfully to Members that comparisons must avoid oversimplification.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Because we have to remember that CNA is mainly our national broadcaster as well as digital news channel, whereas most of the titles in SPH Media Trust (SMT), most of the assets of SMT, are print still – even though they have digital versions – and they are meant to be national papers of record.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And it is perhaps, again, my humble suggestion to Members to look at the performance of public service media holistically.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Because, in truth, we need all of them to reach as many Singaporeans as we can.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that is something to keep in mind.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And as mentioned, both CNA and The Straits Times remained the top-frequented new channels.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And Members who expressed concern about the sustainability of Public Services Media will agree with me that the KPIs, such as reach, are important but they are not the only ways for us to assess the performance and the effectiveness of PSM entities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Equally, we must look at the trust levels that they are able to harness from the population and we must also look at satisfaction levels.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And so, those would be the additional KPIs that we are looking to introduce.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Meanwhile, let me also point to the threat to broadcast television, with consumers shifting to platforms like YouTube or Netflix.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even when PSM entities go onto these platforms, the experiences abroad suggest that placements and algorithms in the digital environment disadvantaged them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Given the important role of our PSM entities to inform, educate and connect Singaporeans, we must be very concerned about their visibility being obscured by the decisions of third-party platforms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Chairman, Singapore is a highly open and digitalised country.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Singaporeans can access information from various platforms – whether it is Xiaohongshu (小红书), Facebook, Netflix, or iQiYi (爱奇艺), these are platforms that many Singaporeans are familiar with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, with more information received, is our ability to discern information sharpened or weakened?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Is the society becoming more united or increasingly divided?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, in an era of intensifying geopolitical competition, being limited in our ability to share our narratives is not beneficial for maintaining our national stance and sense of identity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In this aspect, Public Service Media, such as Mediacorp and Lianhe Zaobao, play crucial roles.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Of course, threats to social cohesion are not the only concern in the digital age.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, some have asked me, given the dangers in the digital world, should Singapore slow down or pause its digitalisation efforts?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Indeed, while Singapore is very safe in the physical world, the digital world has no clear borders and is full of risks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, Singapore is a small country with limited resources.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In an era of intense global competition, digitalisation is key to overcoming our limitations and enabling us to continue thriving.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the digital journey, not progressing is akin to falling behind.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government must therefore adopt the wise strategy of helping citizens and businesses enhance their digital skills and strengthening their cybersecurity awareness.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Only then can Singapore grasp new opportunities in the digital age and our workers can move forward and secure better employment opportunities.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Members for their cuts and questions, and I hope in my response today to be addressing the cuts filed by Ms Jessica Tan, Ms Tin Pei Ling, Mr Ong Hua Han, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Dennis Tan and Ms Mariam Jaafar.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our citizens and businesses must be confident that the digital systems and services that they rely on and the interactions and transactions that they engage in, can be trusted.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I will explain MDDI's approach to building this trust: by ensuring the resilience, security and future-readiness of key digital infrastructure, and by driving Government AI adoption and innovation for the public good.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Government has existing regulations to reduce risks to digital infrastructure and services, including cyberattacks and service disruptions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, under the Telecommunications Act, IMDA requires broadband and mobile network operators to take proactive measures to minimise disruptions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are also sectoral regulations for digital services, such as the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS') IT resilience and security requirements for financial institutions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the digital landscape is much bigger and constantly evolving.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Digital infrastructure, like data centres and cloud services, have become important in enabling many functions including e-banking and payments, ride-hailing, e-commerce and digital identity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These functions allow citizens to meet their day-to-day needs and to do so conveniently and effectively.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, the growing scale and complexity of our digital infrastructure also means an increased surface area for cyberattacks and a higher risk of disruptions arising from hardware failures, misconfigurations and other problems.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Should these disruptions occur, the impact is higher, given the increasing utilisation of these services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Last year, we amended the Cybersecurity Act to address new challenges in our operating environment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These amendments, which are expected to come into force later this year, will empower the CSA to better ensure the cybersecurity of important entities and systems beyond the critical information infrastructure (CII).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This, in turn, improves trust and confidence in Singapore and our digital economy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Owners of CII also have the opportunity, we hope, to review their business models.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We hope that they will be encouraged to review their business models and do so with a view to using new technologies, such as commercial cloud solutions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Beyond cyber threats, we must guard against risks that disrupt access to digital infrastructure and services, including physical hazards like fires; and less visible risks, like hardware failure and system misconfiguration.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These are risks as a result of our dependence on digital infrastructure and services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are studying requirements for major operators to report disruptions to the Government, so that we can better learn and improve from these incidents, and support response and recovery efforts where needed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have been seeking feedback from digital infrastructure providers and some of their customers, since mid-2024.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: IMDA recently released Advisory Guidelines for cloud service providers and data centres.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These guidelines contain key measures that we have been consulting stakeholders on.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The guidelines encourage data centre operators to have a robust business continuity system and ensure high availability for their enterprise customers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Cloud service providers are also encouraged to manage data security risks and ensure business continuity planning.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: All operators are encouraged to implement the measures and many providers, including Microsoft, Equinix and Keppel, and their enterprise customers, have expressed support for the new Advisory Guidelines, which they find to be fit for purpose and aligned with international standards.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are also strengthening the resilience of our Government systems to ensure that Singaporeans have trust and confidence when interacting with the Government online.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have improved the resilience of central systems used by agencies.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to increase the adoption of tools to improve the resilience of Government applications, including those that monitor system uptime.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As resilience measures incur costs, our approach must be calibrated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will support agencies providing important services to implement more sophisticated measures where appropriate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is a need for Government to manage access to information about individuals, as such information could be exploited in scam tactics.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are committed to ensure that data, including personal data, is managed carefully and responsibly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In the Government's provision of digital services involving data, agencies must assess the right balance between the benefits and risks in each use case, to achieve the dual objectives of service accessibility and data protection, in line with the guidelines and safeguards that MDDI has provided.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Last year, we announced that IMDA is investing up to $100 million to upgrade our Nationwide Broadband Network (NBN).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This will enable broadband speeds up to 10 times faster than what most households have today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Operators are starting to offer higher speed broadband services at lower prices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Developing our future-ready digital infrastructure also entails addressing resource constraints as we pursue growth.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We must explore ways to support Singapore's AI ambitions while keeping to our climate commitments, as well as balance digital infrastructure growth with environmental sustainability.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, the Building and Construction Authority (BCA)-IMDA Green Mark for data centres was refreshed last October to raise the bar for data centre sustainability.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: IMDA also launched the Energy Efficiency Grant for the data centre sector last December to support businesses' upgrades to more energy-efficient IT equipment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: MDDI is further exploring ways to uplift data centre sustainability through regulations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are studying other jurisdictions and are in early engagement with the industry to develop a framework for Singapore’s context.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We must continue to build the capabilities for the public sector to create and experiment with AI and unlock citizen-centric solutions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have made available, within the Public Service, access to best-in-class AI and large language model (LLM) tools.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Last year, we organised a whole-of-Government prompt engineering competition.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The fact that I can say this already makes us quite unusual in terms of how we do Digital Government – that we have a prompt engineering competition within Government and there were 1,040 public service officers who participated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The finalists were tasked to build an event publicity website within 10 minutes using large language model (LLM) tools.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The winner of this competition was Muhammad Naim Bin Zahari, a firefighter with the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At the time of the competition, he had just completed a 24-hour shift.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In second place was Rachel Tiang, a finance officer at the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Neither were in technical roles dealing with AI.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Both of them and all the competitors were more than capable of building this functioning publicity website within 10 minutes using these AI and LLM-augmented tools.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We actively involve non-technical public officers in creating digital products.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Last year, the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech) held its inaugural series of hackathons for public officers, called the LAUNCH!

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It gathered more than 600 ideas and birthed 26 innovative prototypes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, a team of two primary school teachers and a GovTech officer prototyped an AI tool to provide students with immediate customised feedback on their oral skills performance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are also exploring how officers can innovate better and faster with AI.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: One of the prototypes from our recent Hack for Public Good hackathon was Spaceship, a tool to make prototyping less daunting for public officers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This tool, Spaceship, enables officers to use AI agents to build and deploy fully functional prototype applications, including LLM-based tools.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, this is a tool for public officers, non-technical public officers to get from an idea to a workable app in minutes using just plain English.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It put the appropriate filter into the spreadsheet, but I think that is the limit of the technology today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As we increase the use of AI in Government, it is critical to understand and mitigate the risks in AI applications.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: GovTech is building the capabilities to ensure that the Government's Gen AI applications go to market safely.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have Litmus, a tool for AI safety and security testing.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have curated a set of tests to ensure our AI applications are resistant to risks that mislead users or cause reputational harm.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Based on tests with agencies, we have seen how Litmus can spot potential safety issues ahead of time, allowing us to act proactively.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Essentially, this is AI testing as a service.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Litmus provides a diagnosis of the AI risks, but we also need a solution, once those risks are detected.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Product teams can choose from a curated list of guardrails, including those from top AI developers and localised ones like LionGuard, and easily integrate these into their applications.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Sentinel has been able to accurately identify attempts to infiltrate systems or trick AI models into producing inappropriate output.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Litmus and Sentinel demonstrate how we want to develop Government Gen AI applications that are safe for use, including by members of the public.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have, therefore, actively invested in enhancing the security, resilience and future-readiness of our key digital infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We also continue to build capabilities in the public sector and embrace experimentation and innovation with AI to better serve Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I am hopeful that this will build trust in our digital future as we continue on our Smart Nation journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Chairman, we want Singaporeans to benefit from good jobs, good wages and better work environments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: To achieve these goals, our enterprises must be competitive amidst rapid digitalisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are doing more to help our workers and enterprises ride the next wave of digitalisation, particularly in AI, through the NAIS 2.0 and the Digital Enterprise Blueprint (DEB) launched last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling and Mr Sharael Taha asked about the progress of NAIS 2.0.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Last year, more than 26 AI Centres of Excellence were set up to push the frontiers of AI innovation and use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For example, Lilly's Digital Health Innovation Hub will accelerate research and development of AI-powered digital health technologies, helping doctors better understand patient needs and provide personalised care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Another example, in the financial services, Prudential's global AI Lab incubates tools to enhance customer experience and improve staff efficiency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The Lab will also partner Institutes of Higher Learning to provide students with opportunities for hands-on-learning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The Enterprise Compute Initiative announced by the Prime Minister in his Budget Speech will help anchor more Centres of Excellence in Singapore and support more innovative AI applications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
